topic: how applications are read (transcript/rigor, testing, additional info)
speaker_role: two former admissions officers turned counselors at College Essay Guy (one previously at Pomona, per transcript)
commercial_incentive: Yes: webinar ends with a pitch for paid counseling/essay packages ($250 off offered), alongside free resources and a pay-what-you-can and free low-income program.
key_insights: Readers judge a transcript against what the student's own school offered, asking what was available and what the student passed up; context (school profile, past applicants) drives the evaluation.
Academics are usually reviewed first as a viability gate; strong grades in rigorous courses are the ideal, and straight A's in easy classes read weaker than B's in hard ones.
Aim for close to four years in each of English, math, science, social studies and language; dropping a language is acceptable if replaced by another core academic course, not a study hall.
Use the additional-information section to explain course choices, gaps, dips or limited offerings with specifics and growth, rather than leaving the reader to guess.
Ask your counselor for your school profile early to see how your school and its grading distribution are being presented to colleges.
Submit a test score if it falls within or above a school's middle 50%; withhold if clearly below and grades are strong; a score far above your school's average can help.
Check each school's policy wording (no-harm, test-blind, flexible, or 'optional' with Common Data Set signals of importance) since 'optional' varies in practice.
Ninth grade gets some leniency, eleventh grade is the key year, and senior-year grades still matter; offers can be rescinded after a sharp drop.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speakers cite NACAC data: colleges calling testing considerably important fell from 46% (2018) to about 5%.
Speakers say over 800 schools went test optional during COVID and only about 15 reverted; over 90% of ranked US colleges do not require tests; about 75% of merit-aid colleges do not require scores.
Common Data Set sections C9 (score ranges) and C7 (importance of testing) recommended as lookup sources.
Speaker says 11 of the top 20 ranked schools returned to test required.
Readers described as handling 60+ applications per day during peak reading.
Suggested testing timeline: PSAT/practice tests in 10th, prep starting summer before 11th, official test by end of 11th, diminishing returns after about three sittings.
notable_or_distinctive: Concrete framework of 'what was available vs. what was left on the table' plus worked examples of reading real school profiles and transcripts.
reliability_notes: Long live-webinar auto-captions with minor garbling; testing statistics are self-described as somewhat dated and the session ends with a sales pitch, but the substantive advice is specific and internally consistent.
